$$\therefore\ x = 1$$

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}$ simplifies to $xy$.
Hence or otherwise, show that $\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding and substituting the given $x^2+y^2=14xy$:
$$\begin{aligned}&\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{x^2+2xy+y^2}{16}\\&=\dfrac{14xy+2xy}{16}\\&=\dfrac{16xy}{16}\\&=xy\end{aligned}$$

Using the log laws $\log a+\log b=\log ab$ and $n\log a=\log a^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\left(\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\right)\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ LHS $=$ RHS, as required.

Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\sqrt{xy}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\text{LHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{RHS}&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\log\left(\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(xy)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{(x+y)^2}{16}\right)&&\text{from part (a)}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log(x+y)^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\log16\\&=\log(x+y)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}-\log16^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log(x+y)-\log4\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$
Alternative method:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(\log x+\log y)\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log x+\dfrac{1}{2}\log y\\&=\log x^{\frac{1}{2}}+\log y^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\\&=\log(xy)^{\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log xy\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^2\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)^{2\times\frac{1}{2}}\\&=\log\left(\dfrac{x+y}{4}\right)\\&=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve $\log_2 x+\log_2(x-3)=2$.

$$\therefore\ x=4$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2\left(2-2x\right)=\log_{\sqrt{2}}\left(1-x\right)$.

solutions.latex:
Both logarithms need $1-x>0$, so $x<1$.

Method 1 (change of base to $\ln$). Using $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$ and $\ln\sqrt{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{\ln(2-2x)}{\ln2}&=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\ln\sqrt{2}}\\ &=\dfrac{\ln(1-x)}{\frac{1}{2}\ln2}\\ &=\dfrac{2\ln(1-x)}{\ln2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\ln(2-2x)&=2\ln(1-x)\\ 2-2x&=(1-x)^2\\ 2-2x&=1-2x+x^2\\ x^2&=1\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
Since $x<1$, $x=1$ is rejected. Check $x=-1$: $\log_2 4=2$ and $\log_{\sqrt{2}}2=2$.
$$\therefore\ x=-1$$
Method 2. Let $y$ be the common value, so $2-2x=2^y$, that is $1-x=2^{y-1}$, and $1-x=\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^y=2^{\frac{y}{2}}$. Equating the two expressions for $1-x$:
$$\begin{aligned}2^{y-1}&=2^{\frac{1}{2}y}\\ y-1&=\dfrac{1}{2}y\\ y&=2\end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $1-x=2^{y-1}$ gives $1-x=2$, so $x=-1$.

parts.latex: Solve $e^{2\ln x} = 4x + 21$

solutions.latex:
Use $e^{2\ln x}=e^{\ln x^2}=x^2$, valid for $x>0$.

$$\begin{aligned} x^2&=4x+21 \\ x^2-4x-21&=0 \\ (x-7)(x+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $x=7$ or $x=-3$.

The original equation needs $x>0$ for $\ln x$, so $x=-3$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ x=7$$

parts.latex: What is the solution of $4^m = 27$ ?

solutions.latex:
Take logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_e 4^m &= \log_e 3^3 \\ m\cdot 2\log_e 2 &= 3\log_e 3 \\ m &= \dfrac{3\log_e 3}{2\log_e 2} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Simultaneously solve the equations $\log_{10}(2-x)-\log_{10}y=1-\log_{10}2$ and $\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y$

solutions.latex:
Rearrange the first equation using log laws.
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(2-x)+\log_{10}2-1 &= \log_{10}y \\ \log_{10}(4-2x)-1 &= \log_{10}y \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$
$$\log_{10}2x=\log_{10}y \qquad (2)$$
Substitute (2) into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{4-2x}{2x}\right) &= 1 \\ \dfrac{4-2x}{2x} &= 10 \\ 4-2x &= 20x \\ x &= \dfrac{2}{11} \end{aligned}$$
From (2), $y=2x=\dfrac{4}{11}$.
$$\therefore\ x=\dfrac{2}{11},\ y=\dfrac{4}{11}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following expressions is equivalent to $4+\log_2 x^2$ ?

parts.latex:
Show that

$$\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$$

Hence, solve the equation

$$6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5=0$$

solutions.latex:
To prove: $\log_a b=\dfrac{1}{\log_b a}$.

Using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\log_c b}{\log_c a}$, with base $c=b$:
$$\begin{aligned} LHS &= \log_a b \\ &= \dfrac{\log_b b}{\log_b a} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_b a} \\ &= RHS \end{aligned}$$

By part (a), $\log_x 2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2 x}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} 6\log_x 2+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ \dfrac{6}{\log_2 x}+\log_2 x-5 &= 0 \\ 6+(\log_2 x)^2-5\log_2 x &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Let $u=\log_2 x$:
$$\begin{aligned} u^2-5u+6 &= 0 \\ (u-3)(u-2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
so $u=3$ or $u=2$.

For $\log_2 x=3$: $x=2^3=8$.

For $\log_2 x=2$: $x=2^2=4$.
$$\therefore\ x=4 \text{ or } x=8$$

parts.latex: When evaluated, $\log_3 100$, lies between which pair of consecutive integers ?

solutions.latex:
Since $3^4 = 81$ and $3^5 = 243$, and $81 < 100 < 243$, the value of $x$ in $3^x = 100$ lies between 4 and 5.

Alternatively, by the change of base rule:
$$\log_3 100 = \dfrac{\ln 100}{\ln 3} \approx 4.2$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_{10}(x - 21) = 2 - \log_{10}x$.

solutions.latex:
The logarithms need $x-21>0$ and $x>0$, so $x>21$.

Collect the logs on one side:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_{10}(x-21)+\log_{10}x &= 2 \\ \log_{10}[x(x-21)] &= 2 \\ x(x-21) &= 10^2 \\ x^2-21x-100 &= 0 \\ (x-25)(x+4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=-4$ or $x=25$.

Since $x>21$, $x=-4$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ x = 25$$
